The Southern brown bandicoot, Isoodon obesulus, is a medium-sized marsupial inhabiting dense heathlands and forests along the eastern and south-eastern coasts of Australia. Newborn offspring are remarkably altricial, with neonates weighing a mere 0.35 grams [Wwb = a mere 0.35 grams] at parturition, a value that reflects the extremely short gestation typical of the Peramelemorphia. In this species, the gestation period lasts for 15 days [tg = 15 days] under standard laboratory conditions maintained at a thermal optimum of 35.9 °C [T = 35.9 °C]. Following birth, the minuscule young crawl to the pouch where they attach to a teat for an extended period of maternal nourishment. The relatively long dependency period, during which the offspring relies entirely on milk, is a critical phase for somatic growth until the time of nutritional independence. This initial mass, barely half a gram, underscores the substantial investment required to carry the litter through the protracted lactation stage that defines the early life history of this peramelid.

Pouch young remain continuously attached to the teat until they reach a sufficiently developed stage to begin exploring the external environment. The time since birth at weaning, when the juvenile permanently leaves the pouch and transitions to a diet of solid food, occurs at 62 days since birth [tx = 62 days since birth] under optimal thermal conditions at 35.9 °C [T = 35.9 °C]. At this critical developmental milestone, the offspring have achieved a wet weight of 125 grams [Wwx = 125 grams], representing a substantial increase from the birth weight as a result of efficient milk transfer. This weaning mass is not the final adult size, as juveniles continue a period of independent foraging and rapid growth before reaching their ultimate dimensions. The nutritional emancipation at this stage marks the end of direct maternal investment in lactation, though the juveniles may remain in the maternal home range while they continue to grow and learn optimal foraging strategies.

Reproductive activity in female Isoodon obesulus is notably prolific for a marsupial of this body size. Throughout their reproductive lifespan, breeding females typically produce 2.73 pups per litter [N_R_i = 2.73 pups per litter] and can sustain a high frequency of typically 2.2 litters per year [F_R_i = typically 2.2 litters per year] when conditions are favorable in a thermoneutral environment at 35.9 °C [T = 35.9 °C]. This combination of moderate litter size and rapid sequential breeding allows for a remarkably high annual output. The ability to rear over two litters annually is critical for population persistence in the face of significant predation pressure, particularly from introduced foxes and feral cats. Such a fast reproductive tempo is characteristic of a species adapted to a high-mortality environment, where maximizing per-capita output offsets the relatively low survival rates of juveniles and adults in the wild.

Sexual maturation in females occurs relatively early in the lifespan, allowing individuals to contribute to the next generation soon after completing their own growth. Puberty is attained at 210 days after birth [tp = 210 days after birth] under a stable ambient temperature of 35.9 °C [T = 35.9 °C], a value that ensures the reproductive system develops according to a predictable schedule. This relatively early onset of reproductive capability, at just under seven months of age, enables females born early in the breeding season to breed within their first calendar year. Such a life-history strategy is typical of small-to-medium-sized marsupials that experience a short window of favorable climatic conditions for rearing young. Reaching sexual maturity rapidly allows the species to maximize its lifetime reproductive output even if individual longevity is curtailed by environmental pressures or senescence.

Maximum longevity in this species, recorded under controlled captive conditions at a constant temperature of 35.9 °C [T = 35.9 °C], reaches 6.5 years [am = 6.5 years], though wild individuals typically have significantly shorter lifespans. The wet weight of a fully grown adult in peak condition reaches 700 grams [Wwi = 700 grams], a mass that is attained gradually through the juvenile and sub-adult stages after weaning. Comparative data from similar-sized peramelids suggest that this ultimate body mass of 700 grams [Wwi = 700 grams] is typical for the genus, though local environmental conditions can cause variation of one hundred grams or more. The balance between a relatively short lifespan and a high reproductive rate is a classic feature of a species occupying a lowland, frequently disturbed habitat where the ability to colonize new areas quickly is highly advantageous. Field studies indicate that senescence may begin as early as three years of age [am = three years of age], with a noticeable decline in body condition and reproductive performance.
